context.title: Problem and context
context.body: Imane Haissam and I developed this graduation project at the Centre de Développement des Énergies Renouvelables (CDER). We had historical SCADA measurements and no continuously connected physical turbine for demonstrations.

objectives.title: Project objectives
objectives.body: We aimed to flag potentially faulty turbine components through multi-label classification and forecast power production. The forecast was intended to help identify lower-production periods for maintenance planning.

architecture.title: System architecture
architecture.body: The simulator sends measurements through an MQTT broker to the Next.js web application. The application forwards inference requests over HTTPS to the Flask API on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano. On the device, the pipeline preprocesses the measurements, constructs time-series windows, and runs the selected models. Predictions return through the API to the web application. The dashboard displays operational measurements, fault classifications, and power forecasts. The administration interface uses the same Flask backend for model lifecycle operations.

contributions.title: My individual contributions
contributions.body:
I designed the software architecture and communication workflow, built the simulator, dashboard, and administration interface, and integrated the models with the application. I designed the MQTT exchanges and configured the Jetson Nano environment.

I also worked on time-series exploration, preprocessing, feature engineering, and evaluation, focusing on statistical and traditional machine-learning methods. I contributed to the team’s deep-learning experiments and comparisons. I wrote the report chapter on time-series analysis and the sections on software architecture and design.

implementation.title: Technical implementation
implementation.body:
The simulator loads historical SCADA measurements from CSV. A user can select a turbine and starting sample, set the replay rate, and pause or resume transmission. The measurements are published in order so the rest of the system receives a stream during tests and demonstrations.

The classification experiments compared CNN, LSTM, RNN, and Random Forest models. The forecasting experiments covered LSTM, CNN, ARIMA, Prophet, and KNN. The team used feature engineering and multivariate time-series preprocessing, and explored MSTL decomposition for forecasting. Source measurements were recorded every ten minutes. For forecasting, we resampled them hourly and produced 24 hourly predictions over a 24-hour horizon.

decisions.title: Engineering decisions
decisions.body:
The simulator let us replay the same input at different rates to test the MQTT-to-dashboard path without access to a live turbine. Historical replay made demonstrations repeatable. Live acquisition would still need testing to assess behavior under real operating and network conditions.

The administration interface separated training and evaluation from activation. Administrators could compare metrics and keep the current model or activate another version. This made model changes reviewable and put the release decision in the administrator’s hands.

Next.js coordinated inference requests, and one Flask backend on the Jetson Nano handled model execution and lifecycle operations. That kept model management in one place for the prototype. The trade-off was that inference depended on the web-to-Jetson connection and the availability of a single backend.

results.title: Results and limitations
results.body:
The prototype demonstrated the path from replayed SCADA measurements to fault predictions and power forecasts in the dashboard. The evaluation used a documented 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% test split. One tuning example passes variables named X_test and y_test as validation data. The original experiment partitions need to be checked to confirm whether the final test set was kept separate from tuning.

A follow-up evaluation should verify that the partitions are strictly separated in time, that preprocessing is fitted only on training data, and that overlapping windows do not cross partition boundaries. It should also check for possible look-ahead effects in MSTL decomposition and measure generalization across unseen turbines and operating conditions.

retrospective.title: Architecture Retrospective: What I Would Design Differently Today
retrospective.body:
The graduation prototype used a single Jetson Nano backend. Today I would investigate a local inference service at each turbine, fed by sensors or SCADA. It would send fault predictions and power forecasts to a central platform for fleet monitoring, history, alerts, and model management. Local inference could continue during upstream interruptions, isolate failures, and scale across the fleet. The trade-offs are additional hardware and maintenance and more complex deployment, security, monitoring, and rollback.

I would evaluate a shared fleet model with controlled turbine-specific calibration or adaptation, given the limited data available for individual turbines and the need to generalize across operating conditions. Online retraining can cause catastrophic forgetting, reinforce unreliable pseudo-labels, and degrade performance. I would require centralized evaluation, approval, versioning, and rollback for model updates. This design was outside the original project and remains unvalidated.

context.title: Project goal and vision
context.body: QubeLink began as a modular smart-home concept: one React Native app would control multiple sockets connected to household appliances. Our team developed the project at ESI Alger between April and June 2024. The physical demo used a single socket to switch one light bulb.

implementation.title: Implemented prototype
implementation.body: The MQTT broker routed messages over Wi-Fi. The ESP8266 firmware interpreted the commands, controlled the relay output, and could report that output’s state on request. The prototype had a power LED and a separate LED for the MQTT connection. The team also worked on a React Native app.

contributions.title: My contributions
contributions.body: I contributed substantially to the ESP8266 firmware, including Wi-Fi setup and LED feedback, and worked on device connection in the mobile app. Circuit design, assembly, soldering, enclosure design and 3D printing, and physical integration were shared team work.

decisions.title: Engineering decisions
decisions.body: A Wi-Fi setup portal let users configure the device and specify a broker address. The connection LED provided feedback on whether the firmware reached the MQTT broker. The enclosure’s closing mechanism failed, so we glued it shut. That made it harder to reopen for repairs.

results.title: Results and limitations
results.body: The demonstration covered a single load: a light bulb. Other appliances, especially motor-driven loads, can draw higher startup currents. Supporting them would require reviewing relay ratings, insulation, strain relief, thermal design, and enclosure materials, followed by appropriate testing. The exact app-to-device path, app state synchronization, and control outside the local network remain unverified. The power LED was present, but the firmware does not establish how it was wired. Voice commands were planned for the app and remained unimplemented.

retrospective.title: What I Would Design Differently Today
retrospective.body:
For a small local-first prototype, I would consider a lightweight HTTP server on each ESP8266. The app could talk directly to each socket over local Wi-Fi to read its reported state, request an on/off change, or retrieve device and connection information. Removing the broker would simplify basic local control. The app would still need to discover and authenticate to devices, manage connections, and keep its displayed state in sync. MQTT would remain useful for central automation, asynchronous updates, and larger installations. Nearby BLE control would require compatible hardware such as an ESP32 because the ESP8266 lacks BLE.

I would add a physical button as a fallback when the app or network is unavailable, provided the microcontroller and firmware are still running. One state mechanism would handle commands from the app, button, and any enabled sensor, with explicit priorities for conflicts. The app would distinguish the reported relay control state from measured power or actual appliance operation. I would also make the enclosure reliably reopenable, review component placement and heat dissipation, and preserve electrical protection around any openings.
